title: Indian-Origin NASA Astronaut Anil Menon Begins First Mission Aboard ISS
excerpt: The Kerala-rooted emergency physician and U.S. Space Force colonel arrived at the International Space Station on July 14 for an eight-month research mission, becoming the latest person of Indian heritage to reach orbit.
body:
• Anil Menon, born in Minneapolis to an Indian immigrant father from Kerala and a Ukrainian immigrant mother, launched to the ISS aboard Soyuz MS-29 on July 14, 2026.
  • The emergency medicine physician and U.S. Space Force colonel will spend eight months conducting research on semiconductor crystals, blood flow in microgravity, and bioprinting.
  • NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman attended the Baikonur launch — the first visit by a NASA chief to the Russian-operated cosmodrome since 2018.
  • Menon's wife, Anna Menon, is also a NASA astronaut who flew on SpaceX's Polaris Dawn mission in 2024, making them one of spaceflight's most accomplished couples.

NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Roscosmos cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina arrived safely at the International Space Station on July 14, completing a three-hour journey aboard the Soyuz MS-29 spacecraft after launching from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.

The spacecraft lifted off at 10:47 a.m. EDT and docked with the station's Prichal module roughly three hours later, bringing the orbiting laboratory's crew to 10. The mission marks Menon's first spaceflight, and he will serve as a flight engineer for Expeditions 74 and 75 during an approximately eight-month stay through April 2027.

From Kerala Roots to the Cosmos

Menon, 49, was born and raised in Minneapolis, Minnesota, to Shankaran Menon, an Indian immigrant from Kerala, and Elizabeth Samoylenko, a Ukrainian immigrant. He is the great-grandson of Chettur Sankaran Nair, a prominent figure in India's independence movement who served as president of the Indian National Congress.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Ul_N5SE4A3w

His academic credentials are formidable: a bachelor's degree in neurobiology from Harvard University, a master's in mechanical engineering and a medical degree from Stanford University, and a master of public health from the University of Texas Medical Branch. He completed residencies in both emergency medicine and aerospace medicine.

Before reaching orbit, Menon built a career spanning military service, humanitarian medicine, and the commercial space industry. As a U.S. Air Force flight surgeon, he deployed to Afghanistan in support of Operation Enduring Freedom and transported critically wounded patients. He served with the Himalayan Rescue Association, providing emergency medical care to climbers on Mount Everest. He also spent a year in India as a Rotary Ambassadorial Scholar, studying and supporting polio immunisation programmes — an experience that deepened his connection to his ancestral homeland.

"NASA kind of bridges the gap between some of these different cultures and synthesizes it. As we look at the moon, everyone is going to pursue that as well. I think that NASA is this great synergy for all of that."

— Anil Menon, NASA Astronaut

SpaceX Pioneer Turned Astronaut

In 2018, Menon joined SpaceX as the company's first flight surgeon, where he built the medical organisation that supported the historic Demo-2 mission in 2020 — the first crewed launch of SpaceX's Dragon spacecraft carrying NASA astronauts to the ISS. He also served as a crew flight surgeon for multiple NASA expeditions aboard the station.

https://www.instagram.com/p/Da04FxToL6Q/

NASA selected Menon as an astronaut candidate in December 2021 as part of its 23rd class. He graduated from the programme in 2024 and began mission-specific training, including time at the Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center in Star City, Russia.

His wife, Anna Menon — a former SpaceX lead space operations engineer — flew to space in September 2024 aboard SpaceX's Polaris Dawn mission, a privately funded orbital flight lasting nearly five days. She was subsequently selected as a NASA astronaut, making the couple one of the few married pairs in the astronaut corps.

Research Agenda in Orbit

During his stay, Menon will conduct scientific research spanning several critical areas for future deep-space exploration. He will work on refining in-space production of semiconductor crystals, a process that could enable large-scale manufacturing of components for high-performance computing, artificial intelligence hardware, and medical devices.

As an emergency physician, Menon brings a particular perspective to the station's medical research. He will perform ultrasound investigations using augmented reality and artificial intelligence methods that could eventually eliminate the need for medical support from Earth during long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars. He will also serve as a test subject for studies on how blood flow changes in microgravity and will test bioprinting vascular constructs — research aimed at understanding the ageing process and advancing therapeutic developments.

Diplomatic Significance

The launch carried geopolitical weight. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman travelled to Baikonur for meetings with Roscosmos director Dmitry Bakanov and to watch the launch in person — the first visit to Russia's launch facility by a NASA chief since 2018. The Russia-Ukraine war had largely prevented Isaacman's predecessor, Bill Nelson, from such direct engagement with Russian space officials.

Isaacman, a billionaire private astronaut, has a personal connection to the crew: he flew alongside Menon's wife Anna on the Polaris Dawn mission in 2024.

"His space journey will help promote awareness."

— Prasanth Nair, Gaganyaan Astronaut, Indian Air Force

What It Means for the Diaspora

Menon's mission adds to the growing roster of Indian-origin astronauts who have flown in space, following in the footsteps of Kalpana Chawla, Sunita Williams, and Raja Chari. His Kerala roots, his year spent working on polio eradication in India, and his family's immigrant story resonate with a diaspora community that has produced an outsized number of leaders in science, technology, and medicine.

With India's own Gaganyaan programme advancing toward its first crewed flight and Indian-origin astronauts continuing to fill key roles at NASA, the bridge between India and American space exploration has never been busier. Menon is expected to return to Earth in April 2027.
